blocks.text: My son set my suitcase by the front door and told me I had until Friday to move into a nursing home.
He genuinely believed the house belonged to him.
He had no idea I had sold it six months earlier.
And he certainly had no idea who had bought it.
My name is Margaret, and for forty-eight years, the little yellow house on Willow Lane had been my home.
My husband, Walter, built it himself in 1974.
He didn’t have much money back then, but he had strong hands, patience, and a stubborn determination to give our family something permanent.
I still remembered watching him lay the first bricks.
I remembered the smell of fresh-cut wood.
I remembered our son Greg running barefoot through the unfinished rooms.
“This will be your home someday,” Walter used to tell him.
Apparently, Greg remembered those words.
Three days after his funeral, Greg and his wife, Dana, arrived with a moving truck.
And I was grateful that my son wanted to be near me.
Then Dana complained that the mattress hurt her back.
I moved my things into the sewing room and started sleeping on a folding bed.
She moved Walter’s photographs into a box.
She painted the kitchen without asking me.
And at Thanksgiving, while talking to her sister on the phone, I heard her say:
“It’s nice finally having our own house.”
Every month, he took $300 from my pension.
And somehow, every repair bill ended up being my responsibility.
I kept telling myself they were still my children.
I kept telling myself that family was worth tolerating discomfort.
Then, one night in March, I got up to get a glass of water.
As I walked past the kitchen, I heard Greg talking on the phone.
“She is eighty,” he whispered. “The doctor says she’s getting forgetful.”
“No, she won’t fight us. She doesn’t even know what half her papers say anymore.”
Then I heard him say something that made my knees almost give out.
Instead, I called an old friend of Walter’s.
Harold had been a real-estate attorney before retiring.
For the next several weeks, Harold helped me gather paperwork.
I learned things I should have known years earlier.
It wasn’t for some harmless family document.
They were preparing paperwork that would transfer the property to Greg.
The money was placed where Greg couldn’t touch it.
And I moved into a small apartment across town.
I needed to know what he would do when he believed he still had power over me.
Then yesterday, I came back to the old house.
I wanted to collect the last of Walter’s things.
That’s when Greg set my suitcase beside the front door.
“A nursing home has a bed for you, Mom,” he said. “Sign this house over and leave by Friday.”
Then at Dana, who was standing behind him with her arms crossed.
“First ask the man who owns this house.”
“The only man who ever owned this house was my father. And he’s been dead for two years.”
“Mom, you’re getting old. You don’t remember—”
I reached into my purse and placed a folder on the table.
Before I could answer, someone knocked on the front door.
Because he recognized the voice from the other side.
When I opened it, a tall man stood on the porch.
It was Daniel, Walter’s younger brother.
Walter’s brother had lived across the country for decades.
Greg hadn’t spoken to him since the funeral.
“You sold my father’s house to his brother?”
He opened his toolbox and pulled out an old envelope.
“I’ve been waiting a long time to give you this.”
Walter had written that he knew Greg had always expected to inherit the house.
But Walter had also written that the house belonged to Margaret.
